## Its place in the curriculum

This [introduction to analytical mechanics course](https://ingenieria.unlam.edu.ar/preview.php?seccion=3&idArticulo=510) plays the role of a bridge between:
- basic sciences courses, from which it takes physics, algebra and calculus tools, and 
- specifical area courses, where these tools are applied,

at the [Mechanical Engineering degree](https://ingenieria.unlam.edu.ar/index.php?seccion=3&idArticulo=371) curriculum at the Universidad Nacional de La Matanza.
![analyticalmechanicsLink.png]([embedded image omitted])
### Primary objective

- calculate for a **system of rigid bodies**
    - **dynamics** of each component
    - **strains** of these components
- Physics beyond the mechanics of rigid bodies are not considered here:
    - deformations
    - thermal effects
    - fluid dynamics
    - electromagnetical interactions
## Why name it _Computational Analytical Mechanics_?

- _Mechanics_
    - Physics branch that relates applyied forces to a body with the resulting dynamics.
    - Simple mechanical devices will be modelled as rigid bodies.
- _Analytical_
    - A system of bodies physics can be solved in **vector** form, 
    - or through an approach also employed in physics courses at freshman and sophomore years, the use **energy** balances (kinetical, gravitotorial potential, etc.). 
    - This later is starting for **analytical mechanics**, 
        - that turns out to be much more powerful,
        - and also, through an ingenious mathematical formulation, it **requires way less effort** to solve complex mechanical systems.
- _Computational_
    - The computer will not only perform the calculations, but it will also systematize the entire workflow, making it even more manageable.
### Computational mechanics

[Computational mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_mechanics) systematically integrates the resources of:
- analytical mechanics,
- numerical computation, and
-computer algebra,

to simulate the behaviour of complex mechanical systems—tasks which would be unfeasible using purely analytical methods.

Its scope ranges from modelling simple gear systems to simulating hydrocarbon reservoirs, biomechanical analysis of prostheses, or the design of complex components in the automotive industry.
#### Numerical analysis

![]([embedded image omitted])

[The differential analyzer invented by engineer Vannevar Bush and completed in 1931 by his team at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Boston, United States of America.](https://ub.fnwi.uva.nl/computermuseum/vbush_tbl.html)

- Numerical computation—deriving numerical solutions through algorithms—[originated in Babylonian civilisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_analysis), where it was already executed on clay tablets.
    - Performing numerical calculations on paper amounts to clinging to archaic methods; it is impractical and irrational to carry them out manually today.
- Prior to the digital computer, mechanical-electrical machines were developed to automate numerical computation.
    - Dispensing with automation entails tedious and error-prone processes.
    - The "differential analyser" illustrated represents an emblematic case: its name refers to solving differential analysis problems (derivatives, integrals), the quintessential application of numerical computation.
- Since the mid-20th century, numerical computation has been conducted using digital computers.
    - This tool is indispensable in contemporary engineering.
    - Neglecting instruction in computational utilisation for these purposes undermines students' professional training.

![]([embedded image omitted])  
[Nijolė Jadzevičiūtė, БЭСМ-6 supercomputer operator, Vilna, Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, 1974](https://i.redd.it/puhzo1k4xe371.jpg)
#### Computer algebra

![]([embedded image omitted])

Symbolic integration in [Macsyma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macsyma), Created in 1968, it is one of the oldest computer algebra systems still in use.

- In the early 1960s, several physicists, such as the Nobel Prize winner [Martinus Veltman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schoonschip), wrote in FORTRAN or LISP [computer algebra systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_algebra_system) for:
    - manipulating mathematical expressions in the same way as it is done manually
    - Automatically make simplifications
    - doing Fourier and Laplace transforms
    - calculate expansions in series, and the sum of their truncations
    - to make integration indefinite and with limits,
    - perform matrix operations, etc.
## Technology to employ

- In a traditional course on analytical mechanics
    - the students produce **differential equations** for the previous items,
    - but we can go further using **tools** that are not usually employed in a classroom
### 19th century | Only tools: blackboard and paper

![]([embedded image omitted])

Professor at blackboard c.1935. Very little has changed in the classroom since then.

- Students and professors waste time (and get bored) by copying the same time after time:
    - The professor **copies on the blackboard** theory and examples elaborated from on those found at books or digital sources.
    - All that is **copied to notebooks** by the students. Nevertheless being of paper or a document in a computer, it is used for a "dumb" copying operation.
    - For each exercise, they solve identical models and calculations once and again.
### 1970s | Electronics in the classroom

![calculator]([embedded image omitted])

The scientific pocket electronic calculator Hewlett Packard 35 started a gradual replacement of the slide rule as the computing device of choice for engineers and scientists.

- Before electronic calculators, students' only aids for accelerating arithmetic and trigonometric calculations were slide rules supplemented by logarithm tables.
- Calculators reduced the time and effort these required, though some contemporary teachers prohibited classroom use, arguing students should 'not become dependent on electronics'.
- Most teachers showed greater sense and permitted their use, but failed to adapt their teaching to leverage this technology's potential.
### 2000s | The computer in the classroom

![]([embedded image omitted])

Control Systems Engineering, University of West England, Bristol, United Kingdom, 2012

- Typically used for presenting slideshows or videos, mirroring the function of slide and film projectors from 50 years prior.
- Occasionally employed as paper alternatives for note-taking and arithmetic via word processors or spreadsheets.
- Thus in 21st-century engineering instruction, computers fulfil essentially the same role as 19th-century classroom tools. Pedagogy remains unchanged despite the technology's potential.
- A particular irony, considering the digital computer was invented during the 20th century expressly to solve engineering problems.
### How it is be employed in this course?

- Those who take _ Computational analytical mechanics_...
    - ...they have already passed the __primary school__:
        - They showed that they understand and can do arithmetic calculations manually.
        - Today they solve their arithmetic calculations faster and with fewer errors in a __pocket calculator__.
    - ...they have already passed algebra and calculus course at the __university__:
        - They demonstrated that they understand and can do integral and differential calculations manually as well as spatial (vector) and matrix calculations.
        - Starting today they will perform the same faster and with fewer errors using a **computer algebra system**.
- The computer performs:
    - Symbolic algebra and calculus to generate differential equations for the dynamics of rigid body systems.
    - Numerical calculations to obtain solutions to those differential equations.
    - Graphical presentations to visualise the results of those calculations.
